decisions.title: Sign in the command line tool by an approval in the website
decisions.question: Why does the command line tool sign in with a code that a person approves in the website, and not with a password in the file .env?

statements.text: The command line tool no longer reads a password from the file .env. The command login shows a short code and an address, a person who is signed in to the website approves the code, and the server gives a token to the tool.

sources.quote: no longer reads a password from the file .env
Sign in the command line tool by an approval in the website

statements.text: The issue lists four problems of the old way. Three of them are: the password is in clear text, acting as another person needs a file edit, and each command makes a new session.

sources.quote: The password is in clear text in the file `.env`.
To act as another person, the developer edits the file `.env`, or sets the two variables before each command.
Each command sends two more requests to the server (the sign in and the sign out), and makes a new session each time.

statements.text: The new design means the tool never sees a password.

sources.quote: The tool never sees a password.

statements.text: The issue names three ways to get the credentials: the variables in .env as before, a sign_in command that keeps the session in a file, or one token for each person. It also asks whether the tool should ask for the password in the terminal.

sources.quote: How does the tool get its credentials: the variables in `.env` as today, a `sign_in` command that keeps the session in a file, or one token for each person?
Does the tool ask for the password in the terminal, so that no file holds the password?

statements.text: The issue was created at 16:29 UTC on 20 October 2026, and the pull request was merged at 17:42 UTC the same day: 1 hour and 13 minutes later.
The design follows an earlier design of another project, issue 578 of teamwright.

sources.quote: The design follows [issue #578 of teamwright]

statements.text: Before the change, a live test named the one assumption that could make the design impossible: a process with no password can get its own credential from an approval made in a real browser, and can then read files through the access checks of the real server.

sources.quote: a Node.js process with no password can get its own credential from an approval made in a real browser, and can then read files through the access checks of the real server.

statements.text: The test ran the real server, the real website, and a real browser. It showed that the tool gets a token with the identity of the person who approved, and that the server still limits the files to the folder of that person.

sources.quote: the tool gets its own token without a password, the token has the identity of the person who approved, the server access checks still limit the files to the folder of that person, a token cannot approve another token, and a device secret works once.

statements.text: The final change adds a token that is a session of 30 days, and the commands login, auth status, and logout.

sources.quote: A token is a session of 30 days
new commands `login`, `auth status`, and `logout`

statements.text: No record found says why the two other ways were not chosen. A keyword search of the issue, its comment, the commit message, and the six linked chat sessions found no such sentence. The search is not a full read of the chat sessions.

The live test listed four cases not tested yet and said the full build covers them. The commit message shows tokens that last 30 days and a logout command. It shows no limit on wrong codes, so that case is not confirmed.

sources.quote: opening the approval address while signed out, logout, the expiry of the token, and a limit on wrong codes. The full build covers these.
A token is a session of 30 days

decisions.title: Add an optional comment and an optional author to every write command
decisions.question: Why does every write command accept a comment and an author?

statements.text: Every write command accepts an optional comment and an optional author. The history entry stores both, and the command history shows both.

sources.quote: Every write command accepts an optional comment and an optional author. The history entry stores both, and the command `history` shows both.
Add an optional comment and an optional author to every write command of heidrun_notebook_ctrl

statements.text: A person who reads the history cannot see why a change was made, or who or what made it. This matters most when the document is shared with other people.

sources.quote: A person who reads the history cannot see why the change was made, and cannot see who or what made the change. This matters most when the document is shared with other people.
